name: Pain or burning when peeing
summary: Pain or burning when you pee is most often caused by a urinary tract infection (UTI), especially in women. Mild cystitis can settle within a few days, but some people need antibiotics.
redFlags: Feeling confused, very drowsy or very unwell, with a high or very low temperature
Cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or a fast heartbeat
Not having peed all day
urgentFlags: Pain in your back or side under the ribs
A high temperature, or feeling hot and shivery
Feeling sick or being sick
Blood in your pee
Symptoms in a man, a child, or during pregnancy
Symptoms that are getting worse

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection (cystitis)
commonCauses.detail: Burning, needing to pee often and urgently, and cloudy or strong-smelling pee.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infection
commonCauses.detail: Chlamydia or gonorrhoea can cause pain when peeing, sometimes with discharge.

commonCauses.title: Irritation
commonCauses.detail: Scented soaps, bubble bath or spermicides can irritate the urethra.

commonCauses.title: Thrush
commonCauses.detail: Vaginal or penile thrush can cause stinging when urine touches irritated skin.

commonCauses.title: Prostate or kidney problems
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, prostate infection or kidney stones.

selfCare: Drink enough water so your pee is pale yellow
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
Rest, and use a hot water bottle on your lower tummy or between your thighs
Ask a pharmacist for advice; in some places they can treat uncomplicated UTIs in women
avoid: Sex until symptoms have cleared
Scented soaps, bubble bath and douches
Relying on cranberry products to treat an infection, as there is no good evidence they do
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not improved after 2 to 3 days, or come back after treatment
You get UTIs often
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
You have pain when peeing but no obvious infection

name: Needing to pee a lot
aliases: getting up at night to pee
summary: Needing to pee more often can be caused by drinking a lot, caffeine, an infection, an overactive bladder, prostate enlargement or diabetes. It is worth checking if it does not settle.
redFlags: Being very thirsty and peeing a lot with vomiting, stomach pain, deep or fast breathing, or confusion
Feeling very unwell with a high temperature, confusion or fast breathing
urgentFlags: Pain or burning when peeing, with a high temperature or pain in your back or side
Blood in your pee
Feeling very thirsty, tired and losing weight
Being unable to pee or only able to pass small amounts despite a strong urge

commonCauses.title: Drinking a lot, caffeine or alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Tea, coffee, energy drinks and alcohol make you pee more.

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Usually with burning and an urgent need to go.

commonCauses.title: Overactive bladder
commonCauses.detail: Sudden urges to pee, sometimes with leaking.

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Common in older men, with a weak flow and getting up at night to pee.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes or pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: High blood sugar and pregnancy both cause more frequent peeing.

selfCare: Cut down on caffeine, fizzy drinks and alcohol
Drink normally through the day but less in the 2 hours before bed
Try bladder training, gradually lengthening the time between toilet visits
Do pelvic floor exercises if you also leak urine
avoid: Cutting down drastically on fluids, which can cause dehydration and concentrated, irritating urine
Ignoring frequent peeing with thirst and weight loss
seeDoctorIf: You need to pee more often than usual for no obvious reason
You are getting up several times a night to pee
You have a weak flow, dribbling or a feeling you have not emptied your bladder
You are very thirsty or tired

name: Blood in urine
summary: Blood in your pee can be caused by an infection or kidney stones, but it can also be a sign of something more serious, so it should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Being unable to pee at all
Passing large blood clots or heavy bleeding
Feeling faint, confused or very unwell with a high or very low temperature
urgentFlags: Blood in your pee with pain in your back or side
Blood in your pee with a high temperature or shivering
Blood in your pee after an injury
Passing small blood clots

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Often with burning, needing to pee often and cloudy pee.

commonCauses.title: Kidney stones
commonCauses.detail: Usually with severe pain in the side, back or groin that comes in waves.

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Can cause blood in the pee in older men.

commonCauses.title: Kidney or bladder disease or cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason blood in pee always needs tests.

commonCauses.title: Harmless colour changes
commonCauses.detail: Beetroot, blackberries, some medicines and periods can colour pee red or pink.

selfCare: Think about whether food such as beetroot, a medicine, or a period could explain the colour
Drink enough fluids so your pee is pale
Book a doctor's appointment even if it only happened once
avoid: Ignoring blood in your pee because it has stopped
Taking leftover antibiotics without advice
seeDoctorIf: You have seen blood in your pee, even once
A urine test has found blood
You have a need to pee more often or a weak flow

name: Kidney or side pain
aliases: pain in my side and back
pain under ribs at the back
summary: Pain in your side or back just under the ribs can come from the kidneys, for example a kidney infection or kidney stone, or from muscles. Kidney problems need prompt treatment.
redFlags: Severe pain with a high temperature and shivering, or feeling confused or very unwell
Cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or fainting
Not having peed all day
Sudden severe pain in the back or tummy in someone over 60, especially with fainting
urgentFlags: Pain in your side with a high temperature, feeling sick or being sick
Severe pain that comes in waves and spreads to your groin
Pain in your side with blood in your pee
Pain in your side during pregnancy
Pain in your side with burning when peeing

commonCauses.title: Kidney infection
commonCauses.detail: Pain in the side or back with a high temperature, shivering and feeling sick, often after cystitis.

commonCauses.title: Kidney stones
commonCauses.detail: Severe pain that comes in waves, often spreading to the groin, sometimes with blood in the pee.

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain
commonCauses.detail: Pain that is worse with movement and better with rest, without fever or urine symptoms.

commonCauses.title: Shingles
commonCauses.detail: Burning pain on one side followed by a blistering rash a few days later.

selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids while you arrange to be seen
Paracetamol can help with pain, following the pack instructions
If muscular, gentle movement and heat can help
avoid: Waiting to see if suspected kidney infection gets better on its own
Taking ibuprofen if you have kidney disease, unless a doctor has advised it
seeDoctorIf: You have mild side pain that keeps coming back
You have had kidney stones before and have similar mild pain
Side pain lasts more than a few days without other symptoms

name: Leaking urine
aliases: leak when I cough or sneeze
summary: Leaking urine is common, especially after childbirth, with age and around the menopause. It can usually be improved with pelvic floor exercises and other treatments.
redFlags: New loss of bladder or bowel control with back pain, or numbness around the genitals or bottom
New loss of bladder control with sudden weakness, numbness or confusion
urgentFlags: Leaking with burning when peeing and a high temperature
Leaking because the bladder is overfull and you cannot empty it
Sudden new leaking with pain in your back or side

commonCauses.title: Stress incontinence
commonCauses.detail: Leaking when you cough, sneeze, laugh or exercise, often due to weak pelvic floor muscles.

commonCauses.title: Urge incontinence or overactive bladder
commonCauses.detail: A sudden, strong need to pee and leaking before you reach the toilet.

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Can cause sudden new leaking with burning and urgency.

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Can cause dribbling and leaking in men.

selfCare: Do pelvic floor exercises every day; results usually take a few months
Cut down on caffeine, fizzy drinks and alcohol
Lose weight if you are overweight
Stop smoking, as coughing strains the pelvic floor
Try bladder training to increase the time between toilet visits
avoid: Drinking much less fluid, which can make the bladder more irritable
Putting off getting help because of embarrassment
seeDoctorIf: Leaking urine affects your daily life
Pelvic floor exercises have not helped after 3 months
You also have difficulty emptying your bladder
You have blood in your pee

name: Difficulty peeing or weak flow
summary: A weak flow, straining or dribbling is common in older men and often due to an enlarged prostate. Suddenly being unable to pee at all is an emergency.
redFlags: Being suddenly unable to pee at all, often with a painful, swollen lower tummy
Difficulty peeing with new numbness around the genitals or bottom, or weakness in the legs and back pain
urgentFlags: Difficulty peeing with a high temperature or pain in your back or side
Blood in your pee
Difficulty peeing after starting a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Very common in men over 50, causing a weak flow, straining and getting up at night.

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: A bladder or prostate infection can make peeing difficult and painful.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some cold remedies, antihistamines and other medicines can make it harder to pee.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: A full bowel can press on the bladder.

commonCauses.title: Narrowing of the urethra or prostate cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes that need tests.

selfCare: Cut down on alcohol, caffeine and fizzy drinks, especially in the evening
Take your time when peeing and try peeing again a few minutes later (double voiding)
Treat constipation if you have it
avoid: Over-the-counter decongestants and some antihistamines, which can make it harder to pee
Assuming it is just age and not getting checked
seeDoctorIf: You have a weak flow, straining or dribbling
You feel your bladder does not empty fully
You get up several times at night to pee
You are worried about your prostate

name: Dark, cloudy or smelly urine
summary: Dark pee usually means you need to drink more. Cloudy or strong-smelling pee can also be a sign of a urine infection.
redFlags: Dark pee with confusion, fainting or extreme drowsiness
Not having peed all day
urgentFlags: Dark pee with yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, or pale poo
Cloudy pee with burning, a high temperature or pain in your back or side
Brown or cola-coloured pee after intense exercise or a crush injury, with muscle pain
Dark pee that stays dark even after drinking more

commonCauses.title: Not drinking enough
commonCauses.detail: Concentrated pee is darker and smells stronger.

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Cloudy, strong-smelling pee with burning and needing to pee often.

commonCauses.title: Food and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Asparagus, beetroot, vitamins and some medicines change pee colour or smell.

commonCauses.title: Liver problems
commonCauses.detail: Dark brown pee with yellow skin or eyes can be a sign of a liver or gallbladder problem.

selfCare: Drink enough fluids so your pee is pale yellow
Drink more in hot weather and when exercising
Check whether a new food, vitamin or medicine could explain the change
avoid: Ignoring dark pee that comes with yellow skin or eyes
Using cranberry products instead of getting a suspected infection checked
seeDoctorIf: Your pee stays dark or cloudy for more than a few days despite drinking more
Your pee is frothy or foamy most of the time
You keep getting urine infections

name: Period pain
summary: Period pain is common and is usually felt as cramps in the lower tummy, sometimes spreading to the back and thighs. Self-care usually helps, but severe pain should be checked.
redFlags: Sudden, severe pain in the lower tummy, especially on one side, if you could be pregnant
Severe pain with fainting, dizziness or shoulder-tip pain
Soaking through pads or tampons every hour with feeling faint
urgentFlags: Severe pain with a high temperature or unusual smelly discharge
Pain that is much worse than your usual period pain
Pain with a coil (IUD) fitted and a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Normal period cramps
commonCauses.detail: The womb muscle tightens to shed its lining; pain is often worst in the first 1 to 2 days.

commonCauses.title: Endometriosis
commonCauses.detail: Tissue like the womb lining grows elsewhere, causing severe period pain, pain during sex or pain when pooing.

commonCauses.title: Fibroids or adenomyosis
commonCauses.detail: Non-cancerous growths or changes in the womb that can cause heavy, painful periods.

commonCauses.title: Pelvic inflammatory disease
commonCauses.detail: An infection, often with discharge, pain during sex or a high temperature.

selfCare: Take ibuprofen or paracetamol, following the pack instructions; ibuprofen often works best if started early
Put a heat pad or hot water bottle on your tummy
Take a warm bath or shower
Gentle exercise such as walking, swimming or yoga can help
Stop smoking, as it can make period pain worse
avoid: Aspirin if you are under 16
Taking more painkillers than the pack allows if the pain is not controlled
seeDoctorIf: Your period pain is severe or stops you doing daily activities
Your period pain has changed or got worse
You have heavy periods, bleeding between periods or pain during sex
Pharmacy painkillers do not help

name: Heavy periods
summary: Heavy periods are common and can affect daily life. A doctor can check for a cause and offer treatments, and test for low iron.
redFlags: Soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for several hours, with dizziness or fainting
Very heavy bleeding with a racing heart, breathlessness or feeling faint
Heavy bleeding with severe tummy pain if you could be pregnant
urgentFlags: Bleeding that is heavier than you have ever had and not easing
Heavy bleeding with a high temperature or unusual smelly discharge
Heavy bleeding while pregnant or after a positive pregnancy test

commonCauses.title: No obvious cause
commonCauses.detail: Many people have heavy periods without any underlying problem.

commonCauses.title: Fibroids or polyps
commonCauses.detail: Non-cancerous growths in the womb.

commonCauses.title: Hormone changes
commonCauses.detail: Around puberty, the menopause or with polycystic ovary syndrome.

commonCauses.title: Contraception or medicines
commonCauses.detail: The copper coil and blood thinners can make periods heavier.

commonCauses.title: Endometriosis, adenomyosis or bleeding disorders
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes that may need tests.

selfCare: Keep a diary of how heavy your periods are and how long they last
Use ibuprofen or paracetamol for pain, following the pack instructions
Eat iron-rich foods such as red meat, beans, lentils and green leafy vegetables
Use a heat pad for cramps
avoid: Aspirin for period pain, as it can make bleeding heavier
Putting up with heavy periods that affect your life
seeDoctorIf: You have to change pads or tampons every 1 to 2 hours, or empty a menstrual cup more often than recommended
You pass blood clots larger than about 2.5cm
Your periods last more than 7 days
You feel tired, breathless or look pale
You also have bleeding between periods or after sex

name: Missed or irregular periods
summary: A late or missed period is often caused by pregnancy, stress, weight changes, exercise or contraception. Do a pregnancy test first if you could be pregnant.
redFlags: A missed period with sudden severe tummy pain, especially on one side
A missed period with shoulder-tip pain, fainting or dizziness
A positive pregnancy test with heavy bleeding and severe pain
urgentFlags: A positive pregnancy test with one-sided tummy pain or light bleeding
Being unable to keep food or fluids down

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: The most common reason if you have had sex; a home pregnancy test is accurate from the first day of a missed period.

commonCauses.title: Stress, weight loss or intense exercise
commonCauses.detail: These can stop or delay ovulation.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal contraception
commonCauses.detail: Pills, injections, implants and hormonal coils can make periods lighter, irregular or stop.

commonCauses.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Irregular periods, sometimes with acne, extra hair growth or weight gain.

commonCauses.title: Menopause or thyroid problems
commonCauses.detail: Periods become irregular before the menopause; an over- or underactive thyroid can also affect them.

selfCare: Take a pregnancy test if you could be pregnant
Keep a record of your periods using a diary or app
Look after your wellbeing: eat regular balanced meals and manage stress where you can
avoid: Assuming you cannot get pregnant because your periods are irregular
Herbal products claimed to 'bring on' a period, which are unproven and may be unsafe
seeDoctorIf: You have missed 3 periods in a row and are not pregnant
You are under 45 and your periods have stopped
You are 15 or older and have not started your periods
Your periods are irregular and you are trying to get pregnant
You have bleeding after the menopause

name: Bleeding between periods or after sex
summary: Light spotting can happen with hormonal contraception or around ovulation, but bleeding between periods or after sex should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting or a racing heart
Bleeding with severe tummy pain if you could be pregnant
urgentFlags: Bleeding with a positive pregnancy test
Bleeding with a high temperature, pelvic pain or unusual smelly discharge

commonCauses.title: Hormonal contraception
commonCauses.detail: Spotting is common when starting or changing pills, implants, injections or hormonal coils, or after missing pills.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause bleeding after sex or between periods.

commonCauses.title: Cervical changes or polyps
commonCauses.detail: Small growths or changes on the cervix can bleed, especially after sex.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Bleeding can happen in early pregnancy, including with miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy.

commonCauses.title: Cervical or womb cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason unexplained bleeding should be checked.

selfCare: Do a pregnancy test if you could be pregnant
Keep a diary of when bleeding happens
Make sure you are up to date with cervical screening
avoid: Ignoring bleeding after sex
Assuming spotting is caused by contraception without checking if it continues
seeDoctorIf: You have bleeding between periods or after sex
Spotting on contraception lasts more than 3 months
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
You are 45 or over with new irregular bleeding

name: Bleeding after the menopause
summary: Any vaginal bleeding a year or more after your last period is not normal and should be checked by a doctor. It is often caused by something treatable, but it can be an early sign of womb cancer.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting or a racing heart
urgentFlags: Heavy or continuous bleeding
Bleeding with pelvic pain and a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Thinning of the vaginal or womb lining
commonCauses.detail: Lower oestrogen after the menopause can make the tissues thin and bleed easily.

commonCauses.title: Hormone replacement therapy
commonCauses.detail: HRT can cause some bleeding, especially when starting or changing treatment.

commonCauses.title: Polyps
commonCauses.detail: Small non-cancerous growths in the womb or cervix.

commonCauses.title: Thickened womb lining or womb cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason any bleeding after the menopause must be investigated.

selfCare: Make an appointment with a doctor even if the bleeding was light or happened once
Note when the bleeding happened and how heavy it was
avoid: Waiting to see if it happens again
Assuming it is a period returning
seeDoctorIf: You have any bleeding a year or more after your last period
You have unexpected bleeding while on HRT
You have new vaginal discharge after the menopause

name: Unusual vaginal discharge
summary: Some vaginal discharge is normal and changes during the cycle. A change in colour, smell or texture, or itching, is often due to thrush or bacterial vaginosis, which are easily treated.
redFlags: Discharge with severe tummy pain, a high temperature and feeling very unwell
Feeling faint, confused or very unwell with a high temperature and a tampon or menstrual cup in place
urgentFlags: Discharge with pelvic pain or a high temperature
Discharge with bleeding between periods or after sex
Unusual discharge during pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Bacterial vaginosis
commonCauses.detail: Thin, grey-white discharge with a strong fishy smell.

commonCauses.title: Thrush
commonCauses.detail: Thick, white discharge like cottage cheese, with itching and soreness.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Trichomoniasis, chlamydia or gonorrhoea can cause green, yellow or frothy discharge.

commonCauses.title: Normal changes
commonCauses.detail: Discharge changes with the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, contraception and the menopause.

selfCare: Wash the outside of the vagina gently with water or plain unperfumed soap
Wear cotton underwear and avoid tight clothing
Ask a pharmacist about treatments for thrush or bacterial vaginosis if you have had it diagnosed before and recognise the symptoms
Use condoms with new or casual partners
avoid: Douching or washing inside the vagina
Perfumed soaps, wipes and feminine deodorants
Home remedies such as yoghurt, garlic or tea tree oil inside the vagina
seeDoctorIf: This is the first time you have had these symptoms
Treatment has not worked or symptoms keep coming back
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
You are pregnant, under 16 or have gone through the menopause

name: Itching or soreness in the genital area
summary: Itching and soreness in the genital area is commonly caused by thrush or irritation from soaps. It is usually easy to treat.
redFlags: Rapidly spreading redness, swelling and severe pain in the genital area with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Painful blisters or sores on the genitals
Itching with pelvic pain or a high temperature
Swelling that makes it hard to pee

commonCauses.title: Thrush
commonCauses.detail: Itching, soreness and thick white discharge; can affect women and men.

commonCauses.title: Irritation
commonCauses.detail: Soaps, bubble bath, wipes, washing powders or latex condoms.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Genital herpes, trichomoniasis or genital warts can cause itching.

commonCauses.title: Skin conditions
commonCauses.detail: Eczema, psoriasis or lichen sclerosus can affect the genital skin.

selfCare: Wash with water or plain unperfumed soap and pat dry
Wear loose cotton underwear
Use a plain emollient instead of soap
Ask a pharmacist about thrush treatment if you have had thrush before and recognise the symptoms
avoid: Scented products, douches and wipes
Scratching
Using thrush treatment repeatedly without being checked
seeDoctorIf: This is the first time you have had these symptoms
Symptoms have not improved after 7 to 14 days of treatment
You get thrush more than twice in 6 months
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
You have white patches or skin changes in the genital area

sources.label: NHS: Thrush in men and women

name: Pelvic pain
summary: Pain in the area below your belly button and between your hips is often linked to periods, ovulation or a urine infection. Sudden or severe pelvic pain needs to be checked quickly.
redFlags: Sudden, severe pelvic pain, especially on one side, if you could be pregnant
Pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, fainting or dizziness
Severe pain with a high temperature, vomiting and feeling very unwell
Sudden severe one-sided pain with vomiting
urgentFlags: Pelvic pain with a high temperature or unusual discharge
Pelvic pain with pain or burning when peeing
Pelvic pain with bleeding between periods or after sex
Pelvic pain during pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Period pain or ovulation pain
commonCauses.detail: Cramping around a period, or a one-sided ache mid-cycle.

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Low tummy pain with burning and needing to pee often.

commonCauses.title: Pelvic inflammatory disease
commonCauses.detail: An infection of the womb, tubes or ovaries, often with discharge or pain during sex.

commonCauses.title: Endometriosis or ovarian cysts
commonCauses.detail: Long-term pain that often gets worse around periods.

commonCauses.title: Ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage
commonCauses.detail: Pain with a missed period or positive pregnancy test needs urgent assessment.

selfCare: Do a pregnancy test if you could be pregnant
Use paracetamol or ibuprofen for mild pain, following the pack instructions
A heat pad or warm bath may ease cramping
Keep a diary of when the pain happens and what makes it better or worse
avoid: Waiting at home with sudden severe pain
Assuming new pelvic pain is just period pain if it feels different
seeDoctorIf: You have pelvic pain that keeps coming back or lasts more than a few weeks
You have pain during sex
Your periods have become more painful
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
